summary:
The Criminal Offences Act criminalises same-sex activity between men and women, with a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment. Outright International's overview, updated in March 2026, records no evidence of enforcement in recent years, and the US State Department's 2010 human rights report described enforcement of the sodomy provision as rare. The provision remains in force; the absence of recent prosecutions is not a repeal.

The same Act contains an offence aimed at gender expression rather than private conduct: a male who solicits in public "for an immoral purpose" with intent to deceive as to his true sex commits an offence. Because it turns on how a person appears and speaks in public, it bears on a trans visitor's visible presentation in streets, venues and other public space in a way the sodomy provision does not.

Tonga provides no legal gender recognition. A visitor's passport and other documents will carry the sex marker assigned at birth, and no administrative or judicial procedure exists to change it. There is no route to a Tongan identity document matching a visitor's gender.

No Tongan law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment or in the provision of goods and services. The Judicial Code of Conduct 2010 requires judges to be aware of diversity including sexual orientation and bars bias on irrelevant grounds, but it binds judges alone, not employers, landlords or service providers.

Tongan law does not recognise same-sex relationships or unions in any form. No partnership, marriage or next-of-kin rights appear in the source material. A trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status holds no recognition or spousal standing here.

An LGBTQ activist, Polikalepo Kefu, was murdered near his home at Muʻa in 2021. LGBTQ people in Tonga face a climate of fear, discrimination and homophobia attributed to conservative values, colonial-era laws, and rising fundamentalism and religious fanaticism that has increased hostility toward LGBTQ people and fakaleitis.
tangentialFactors:
Tonga, with Kiribati, is the only Polynesian country that has not signed or expressed support for the 2011 UN joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The government has made no commitment to that framework.

The US State Department's 2010 report listed domestic violence, discrimination against women and corruption as the most prevalent human rights problems in Tonga and recorded no government abuses. That assessment predates the current period and does not address policing of the offences above.
localsOnly: Tonga's only LGBTI drop-in centre and shelter, on Tongatapu in Nukuʻalofa, lost part of its roof to Cyclone Gita in February 2018, when winds exceeded 120 mph. Bathrooms and bedrooms used by LGBTI Tongans were damaged. The country's community shelter infrastructure is a single facility and is exposed to storm damage.
outOfScopeNotes:
No available source records enforcement of the public-solicitation provision, or any prosecution of a trans or gender-nonconforming person under it. Whether police apply it is unresolved.

No sourced information was identified on Tongan border, immigration or airport screening practice as it affects trans travellers, including whether document markers prompt secondary inspection.

No sourced information was identified on hate-crime or sentencing provisions covering anti-LGBTQ violence, or on police response to such violence.

The most detailed enforcement assessment available is the US State Department's 2010 report; its age limits what it establishes about current policing.

Available sources record no partnership, marriage or next-of-kin rights for same-sex couples, but do not document how Tongan authorities would classify a relationship involving a trans person whose documents carry a different sex marker.
